title: The Great Inland Movement: Migration to the Great Lakes, 2080–2140
body:
# The Great Inland Movement: Migration to the Great Lakes, 2080–2140

The largest organized migration in the history of the North American continent was not organized. It had no coordinator, no transport authority, no resettlement program. It was sixty years of individual decisions accumulating into a demographic transformation that rearranged the population of a continent.

## The Shape of It

At the 2080 population estimate, the former United States had approximately 380 million residents. Of these, approximately 110 million lived in metropolitan areas on or within fifty kilometers of the Atlantic coast, and approximately 85 million in comparable proximity to the Pacific. Together, roughly 50% of the country's population occupied geographic zones that would, over the following six decades, become progressively more expensive, more dangerous, or more economically marginal to inhabit.

Not all of these people moved. Many stayed — for reasons economic, emotional, or simply inertial. The ones who moved did not move all at once, and they did not move in a single direction. The migration was centripetal: a general drift from periphery toward interior, from the coasts toward the Great Lakes basin, which sat at the geographic center of the continent with the largest fresh water supply in the northern hemisphere, a climate that was warming but not catastrophically, and agricultural land that was, in some cases, becoming more productive as the growing season extended northward.

The GLMZ received approximately 22 million migrants between 2080 and 2140. The scale of this number is difficult to convey. Twenty-two million people is more than the total population of the GLMZ's predecessor city of Chicago at the beginning of the migration period. The urban infrastructure of the Great Lakes region absorbed this population while simultaneously undergoing the corponation transformation — the two processes occurring in parallel, the corponations claiming territory as the migrants arrived, the migrants navigating a city that was reorganizing itself around them.

## Where They Came From

The migration was not uniform from the coasts. It came in waves, each wave driven by a different threshold.

The first wave, 2080-2095, was predominantly economic. The financial and technology industries' migration to the GLMZ pulled professional workers who followed their employers. These were Tier 3-5 workers in the eventually-established classification system — people whose skills were wanted by the arriving corponations and who arrived into sponsored situations. They are the least discussed migrants because their transition was the most comfortable and their integration the most seamless. They are also the reason the GLMZ's early corponation era had the skilled workforce the corponations required.

The second wave, 2095-2115, was mixed. The insurance markets' exit from coastal real estate, the water pricing crises of the Southwest, the first major fire seasons that consumed communities rather than just wildland — these events produced migrants at all economic levels. The professional migrants of the second wave arrived into a GLMZ that was more developed than the one their predecessors had entered, and less accommodating: the best corponation positions were filled, the easiest Gray Zone territories were occupied, the sponsorship market was competitive. The second wave populated the inner zones of the Gray Zone.

The third wave, 2115-2140, was the largest and the hardest. These were the people who had stayed through the second wave — who had waited, who had hoped, who had resources or attachments or simply the human tendency to stay where you are until the staying becomes impossible. The fires that consumed the communities they thought were safe, the storm seasons that made the cost of coastal insurance rational only for the very wealthy, the water restrictions that crossed the threshold from inconvenience to crisis: these events produced migrants who arrived with less, into a GLMZ that was offering less, in a period when the corponation structure was sufficiently entrenched that entry-level corponation positions were scarce and Gray Zone territories were dense.

These are the people whose children are now the long-term Gray Zone residents of the GLMZ's southern and central zones. Their integration was not integration in the conventional sense. They arrived and they stayed and they built communities in the spaces the corponations had not claimed, and the communities have been there for a hundred years, and they are the Gray Zone.

## What Stayed Behind

The migration that came to the GLMZ was not everyone who could have come. It was everyone who chose to come and had the means to do so. The people who remained in the coastal communities were those for whom the means were absent or the choice was against: the very old, the very poor, the ones whose attachment to place outweighed the economic logic of relocation, the ones who calculated that the risks of the familiar were more manageable than the risks of the unknown.

These people became the Remnants — or rather, they remained in places that, as the corponation era progressed and claimed the economically viable territories, became what is now called the Remnants. They did not fail to migrate and therefore become Remnants. The corponation era created the category of Remnants by creating its own category, and what was not subsumed by the corponation era was, by definition, outside it.

The Remnants are not the failure of the migration. They are the remainder — in the mathematical sense, what is left when one quantity is subtracted from another. The migration happened. The GLMZ absorbed what it absorbed. The rest remained. The rest continues.
